title: How do two numbers compare a picture's width and height?
description: The width and height of the tiger picture are written as one comparison and read in words. Both numbers are then halved to find which picture comes out. Keeko's doubt is that taking the same number off both numbers gives the smaller picture.
teaching_notes: One idea: a ratio compares two quantities, and multiplying both terms by one factor keeps the ratio. Watch for students who take the same number away from both terms.

source: Write the width to height ratio of image A (60 mm by 40 mm)
video_script.why: The child moves from comparing factors of the sides to one comparison of width with height, and sees that halving both terms gives the smaller picture.
video_script.substitution: Write width to height as one comparison, read it in words, then multiply both terms by one half.
video_script.anchor: the book's tiger picture, image A, 60 mm wide and 40 mm high
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko takes thirty away from both terms of sixty to forty and gets thirty to ten. The factors are one half and one quarter, so the shape changes and the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: Halving both terms of sixty to forty gives thirty to twenty, which is image C.

final_answer.spoken: sixty to forty; halving both terms gives thirty to twenty, which is image C

maths_rules: image A: width 60 mm, height 40 mm; width to height is 60 : 40; the terms are 60 and 40
meaning: for every 60 mm of width there are 40 mm of height
multiply both terms by 1/2: 60 × 1/2 = 30 and 40 × 1/2 = 20; the new ratio is 30 : 20, which is image C (30 mm by 20 mm)
Keeko's slip: 60 − 30 = 30 and 40 − 30 = 10 gives 30 : 10; the factors are 30 ÷ 60 = 1/2 and 10 ÷ 40 = 1/4, which differ, and 30 : 10 is not 30 : 20
video_script.design: One idea: a ratio compares width with height, and one factor on both terms keeps it. Assumes the factor of change. Wrong idea: take the same number off both terms. The picture stays for the whole video.

<bookmark mark='pic'/>Image eigh is sixty millimetres wide and forty millimetres high.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How can we compare its width with its height using these two numbers?

narration: <bookmark mark='lift'/>We can put the width and the height side by side as sixty to forty.
<bookmark mark='ratio'/>A comparison of two quantities like this is called a ratio.
<bookmark mark='terms'/>The numbers sixty and forty are called the terms of the ratio.

<bookmark mark='ans'/>Halving both terms of sixty to forty gives thirty to twenty, which is image C.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the new ratio is thirty to ten, because thirty was taken away from both terms.
<bookmark mark='sub'/>Sixty take away thirty is thirty, and forty take away thirty is ten.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But the two terms did not change by the same factor.
<bookmark mark='fac'/>The width became one half of sixty, while the height became only one quarter of forty.
<bookmark mark='land'/>That picture is much flatter than image C, so we multiply both terms by one factor.
